extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity sleuths, and readers interested in publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and assessing problems that warrant expressions of concern or retraction in biomedical publications (e.g., compromised peer review, data mismatches, plagiarism, methodological flaws). Useful for peer reviewers, editors, and research-integrity investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the peer-review process was interfered with or manipulated (page: journal’s investigation found the guest editor for the issue selected the peer reviewers, the majority of whom were affiliated with Nanjing University in China; investigation found evidence of compromised peer review in almost all articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include guest editors or authors selecting reviewers, reviewer pools that are unusually homogeneous or tied to authors, undisclosed reviewer selection practices. Red flags: lack of reviewer independence, undeclared relationships between reviewers and authors, and widespread reviewer overlap across papers in an issue. Investigations can lead to retraction when peer review is judged “irreparably compromised.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreproducible analyses / inability to replicate reported analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Published analyses cannot be reproduced from the provided data/methods (page: apple cider vinegar paper retracted “because the authors’ analyses could not be replicated and multiple errors were identified”; BMJ stem cell study: data/supporting files showed inconsistencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare article results to provided datasets and code; attempt replication where feasible. Red flags: missing or incomplete datasets, analyses that do not match reported results, failure of independent attempts to recreate findings. Journals may issue expressions of concern or retract when replication fails and errors are multiple or fundamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inconsistencies and statistical anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrepancies between the article and its underlying data, or unusual statistical patterns (page: sleuths pointed out a “curious repeating pattern” of records every 101 records; many integer values for height/weight; ‘complete mismatch’ between article and dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine datasets for repeating patterns, improbable distributions (too many round integers), duplicates, or metadata mismatches. Use simple statistical checks (digit-preference tests, duplication checks) and visualizations. Report anomalies to editors and on public forums (e.g., PubPeer) when appropriate; such anomalies have precipitated expressions of concern and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe discrepancies in trial conduct or reporting (e.g., randomization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major inconsistencies in how a trial was run or reported compared to its methods (page: BMJ retracted clinical trial for ‘severe’ discrepancies in randomization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify trial registration, CONSORT adherence, and randomization procedures. Look for implausible baseline balance, inconsistencies between protocol and reported methods, and unexplained deviations. Significant problems in randomization/trial conduct can justify retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undeclared conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors failed to disclose relevant conflicts (page: BMJ acknowledged issues including undeclared conflicts of interest in its expression of concern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require full disclosure statements; scrutinize affiliations, funding sources, and undeclared relationships. Undeclared conflicts that could bias results or interpretations are grounds for expressions of concern, corrections, or retraction depending on severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and self-plagiarism / misrepresentation of references
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual plagiarism, recycling one’s own work without disclosure, or misrepresenting cited material (page: Paul McCrory articles retracted for plagiarism, recycling his own work, and misrepresenting a reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plagiarism-detection tools and manual checks. Look for unattributed reuse, recycled editorials or duplicate text across publications, and references that do not support claims. Proven plagiarism or substantial undisclosed recycling can lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate publication / misrepresentation of data provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing data that were previously published or misrepresenting where/when data were collected (page: authors claimed trial data came from one center but it came from three; data had already been published elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check prior publications, trial registries, and author statements about data provenance. Confirm whether datasets/reporting overlap with earlier work. Duplicate publication or false claims about data origin can prompt retraction or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological flaws and unsound conclusions (guidelines and systematic reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious methodological problems in reviews, meta-analyses, or guidelines that undermine conclusions (page: 34 medical societies called for BMJ to retract a guideline, citing serious concerns about the methodology and conclusions and potential impact on patient care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess risk-of-bias, search strategy, inclusion criteria, meta-analytic methods, and how conclusions are linked to evidence. For clinical guidelines, examine panel composition and conflict disclosures. Flawed methods that materially change recommendations can trigger formal complaints, expressions of concern, or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight failures and delayed corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures by journals/editors to detect problems, to transparently identify responsible editors/authors, or to act promptly on concerns (page: guest editor not named; BMJ removing authors months after sleuths flagged data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should maintain transparent editorial processes (identify guest editors, document reviewer selection), rapidly investigate credible concerns raised by sleuths, and issue timely corrections, expressions of concern, or retractions. Lack of oversight can worsen harm and invite external calls for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public post-publication review channels (e.g., PubPeer) as detection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Community sleuthing and post-publication comments can reveal problems (page: sleuths used PubPeer to flag inconsistencies that led to expressions of concern and retractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat public reports and post-publication peer review as valuable sources of leads. Editors should have processes to evaluate public concerns, request raw data or explanations, and take corrective action when warranted. Encourage transparent dialogue and data sharing to facilitate detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers for expressions of concern versus retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: When journals issue an expression of concern versus proceeding to retraction (page: BMJ placed an expression of concern where issues were “apparent from the data” but further investigation was ongoing; other items were retracted when problems were irreparable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expressions of concern when serious issues are suspected but investigation is incomplete; retract when evidence shows irreparable problems (fabrication, unfixable errors, compromised review). Clearly document the rationale and keep notices linked to the original article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship accuracy and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct attribution and accountability of listed authors (page: BMJ retracted a cardiac stem cell paper and removed authors months after sleuths flagged data ‘mismatch’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require author contribution statements and verification of author approval. Investigate and correct authorship when responsibility for data or analysis is misrepresented; removal or retraction may follow when authorship issues relate to misconduct or unreliable data.
